problem: Turn on the "YouTube Analytics API" in your Google Cloud project, then tap Analyze now again.
summary: The biggest gap is about when a film was posted, not what it was about. Every film older than 5 days got 37 views or fewer (0.8–6.5 views/day), and 9 of the 10 films posted in the last 2.5 days reached 160–2,285 views/day. That makes the best-vs-worst quarter comparison mostly a comparison of two posting periods. Within the recent films, the leaders are hands-on, everyday-object physics with one surprising visible moment (spoon pulled into a stream, egg that keeps spinning, brick caught softly, slipping on ice). Space and weather topics trail them.

working.lesson: Everyday objects doing something surprising that you can see on screen lead the channel.
working.evidence: Best quarter: Coanda spoon 2,285.4/day, Impulse brick 1,292.4/day, Ice slippery 846.9/day, Egg spin test 758.0/day. All four are kitchen, street or worksite objects with a visible physical surprise.

working.lesson: Titles that challenge what viewers expect ('doesn't hurt', 'it's not pressure', 'never lies') are in the top group.
working.evidence: 'Why Catching a Thrown Brick Doesn't Hurt' 1,292.4/day; 'Why Is Ice Slippery? It's Not Pressure' 846.9/day; 'Raw or Boiled Egg? The Spin Test Never Lies' 758.0/day.

working.lesson: A clear 'which one?' setup gets likes.
working.evidence: Hammer vs Feather has the most likes on the channel: 23 likes on 1,234 views. Egg spin test: 12 likes on 379 views.

working.lesson: Familiar winter physics also does well.
working.evidence: Static shock 558.2/day (1,153 views), Ice 846.9/day, Car roof frost 383.4/day.

notWorking.lesson: Biology, plant and body-myth topics sit at the bottom. They also fall outside the channel's stated subjects. This is confounded with posting date, because all of them are 6+ days old.
notWorking.evidence: Why Leaves Change Color 0.8/day, Poinsettia Poison Myth 0.8/day, Head Heat Loss Myth 1.1/day, Cold Weather Makes You Pee 1.2/day.

notWorking.lesson: A broad 'how does X work' topic with no surprise moment did poorly.
notWorking.evidence: 'How Solar Electricity Works' (topic brief: 'How does the solar electricity works?') got 6 views, 0.9/day.

notWorking.lesson: Space and astronomy topics trail kitchen and body physics among the recent films.
notWorking.evidence: Leonid meteor shower 160.4/day and Seasons/axial tilt 326.0/day, against 758–2,285/day for the top four recent films.

notWorking.lesson: Filler hashtags made from plain title words show up only on the weakest films. This is not proven to cause anything, because the same films are also the oldest.
An everyday-physics topic can still stall, so topic alone does not guarantee views.
notWorking.evidence: Buttered toast got 4 views (8.0/day) at 0.5 days old, while Egg spin test, posted the same day, got 758.0/day. It is too early to judge the toast film.

rules: Pick an everyday object (kitchen, home, street, body in motion) that does something viewers don't expect, and show that moment in the first seconds.
Stay on physics and technology. Skip plant biology and human physiology.
Turn 'how X works' topics into a surprise or a contradiction (e.g. 'Why X doesn't do what you think').
Put the contradiction in the title: 'X Doesn't Hurt', 'It's Not Y', 'The Test Never Lies'.
Use a two-option setup when the topic allows it (raw vs boiled, hammer vs feather) and show the answer on screen.
Keep films between 25 and 38 seconds, the range of all four top films.
Use specific hashtags (the effect name, the object, #physics, #science). Never use single filler words from the title like #makes, #need, #works or #head.
Write and save the opening sentence in the hook field for every film, so hooks can be compared next time.
moreTopics: Kitchen physics demos (spoons, eggs, water streams, pans)
Momentum, impulse and inertia in everyday actions (catching, braking, airbags)
Winter physics people feel directly (ice, static shock, frost)
Physics myths with a concrete test on screen
Everyday technology explained through one surprising effect
lessTopics: Human physiology and body myths (urination, head heat loss)
Broad 'how does X work' overviews with no twist
experiments: Check whether the recent jump is a channel-wide change: post one physics film in the old style (a broad 'how it works' topic) next to one surprise-demo film on the same day, and compare their views per day after 3 days.

Test length on purpose: make two similar kitchen-physics films, one at about 28 seconds and one at about 40 seconds. The only 40+ second recent films (Toast at 40s, 8/day; Seasons at 42s, 326/day) trail the field, but they are only 0.5 day…
Test posting hour: post comparable films at 09:00 and at 21:00 on the same weekday. Current hour results are mixed and confounded by film age, so no best time can be named yet.
